item.title: Toward Interpretable Graph-Based Machine Learning for Combustion Kinetic Model Generation
item.description: This work presents an atom-conserving and interpretable graph neural network (GNN) for combustion kinetic model generation, where atoms are represented as nodes, covalent bonds are represented as edges, and reactions are represented as bond-rearrangement operations. Its artificial-intelligence (AI) contribution is a reaction generator that extends a standard Graph Isomorphism Network with Edges (GINE) architecture through reaction-context embeddings, reaction branching & third-body reaction inputs, Arrhenius-rate-parameter prediction, pairwise decoding, and stochastic inference over evolving reactant pools. Trained on the Li–Dryer hydrogen combustion kinetic model (8 species and 21 reactions), the GNN reproduces trained chemistry and generates element-balanced new reactions and intermediate species outside the training dataset, many of which have experimental analogues. When trained on a subset of the Li–Dryer dataset, the model recovered most held-out reactions and revealed relationships between samples (reactions) in the model’s latent space. The results suggest that the model learns transferable local reaction structures and generates valid species and reactions. As with any reaction generators, the generated reaction models require thermochemical and kinetic verification; the intended engineering application is low-cost reaction-pathway exploration for new fuels and prioritization of experiments and first-principles calculations to develop new combustion kinetic models.

item.title: Data-efficient molecular and nanoparticle design via fine-tuned large language models
item.description: Designing molecules with prescribed properties is central to pharmaceutical and materials innovation, but vast chemical design spaces make development lengthy and costly. Generative artificial intelligence can accelerate molecular discovery, but its deployment in many real-world domains remains limited by the need for large task-specific training datasets. To enable generative design when property-labeled data are scarce, we present a data-efficient foundation-model adaptation strategy combining complementary positive and negative property prompts with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Generated molecules are then ranked by molecular graph-kernel Gaussian process regression for structure-aware prioritization. In a controlled computational setting, the platform generated candidates with novel scaffolds satisfying multiple design objectives, including predicted target binding, synthesizability, and drug-likeness. Although only a few hundred training molecules per target met all three criteria, the model generated thousands of new molecules matching the desired profiles. For prospective validation, we applied the model to nanoparticle design, a domain of high clinical potential but limited excipient diversity. Fine-tuning on only 1,521 labeled drug-excipient pairs - including just 139 nanoparticle-forming examples identified new nanoparticle-forming excipients for the anticancer drug sorafenib. The model proposed lithocholic acid and the sorafenib metabolite M6, and experiments confirmed that both form stable sorafenib nanoparticles with high encapsulation efficiency and increased in vitro potency. These findings show that foundation-model fine-tuning with complementary prompts and graph-based prioritization enables data-efficient molecular design in low-data chemical domains.

item.title: Ion Pairing and Electrochemical Behavior of Al(OTf)3 in Propylene Carbonate Bilal Overton
item.description: The development of practical aluminum-ion batteries requires electrolytes capable of stabilizing multivalent aluminum species while maintaining sufficient ionic conductivity and electrochemical activity. Here, we investigate aluminum trifluoromethanesulfonate (Al(OTf)3) dissolved in propylene carbonate (PC) as a potential halide-free aluminum electrolyte using a combined computational and experimental approach. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to optimize coordination structures and predict speciation, redox potentials, and vibrational signatures of solvated aluminum complexes. Cyclic voltammetry reveals electrochemical activity with a reduction onset near 0 V versus Al/Al3+, consistent with computational predictions. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy indicates significant ionic association between aluminum and triflate anions, suggesting the coexistence of free and coordinated species in solution. Scanning electron microscopy of copper substrates after chronoamperometric deposition shows surface features consistent with metal deposition, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms the presence of aluminum-containing species. The electrolyte exhibits an ionic conductivity of approximately 5.4 mS cm-1 at ~0.6 M. These results demonstrate that Al(OTf)3/PC solutions support electrochemical activity of aluminum species but exhibit strong ion association, highlighting key challenges and opportunities for halide-free aluminum battery electrolytes.

item.title: Machine Learning for Ionic Conductivity Prediction in Polymer Electrolytes: A Benchmark on Lithium Systems and a Feasibility Study on the Data-Scarce Multivalent (Mg, Zn, Na) Frontier
item.description: Solid and gel polymer electrolytes are central to safer, more flexible batteries, and machine learning has been used to predict their ionic conductivity directly from composition and processing variables. Almost all of this work targets lithium-ion systems, for which large, curated datasets exist. Polymer electrolytes conducting multivalent or non-lithium cations (magnesium, zinc, sodium) are promising lower-cost alternatives but remain comparably underexplored, in part because no public, ML-ready dataset of their measured ionic conductivities exists. Here we validate a standard composition-to-conductivity pipeline (Random Forest and XGBoost regression) on OBELiX, a published dataset of 599 lithium solid-state electrolytes, reaching R2 = 0.79 against a mean-predicting baseline near zero. We then construct, to our knowledge, the first ML-ready dataset of Mg-, Zn-, and Na-conducting polymer electrolytes, systematically mined from the primary and review literature: 135 data points across 105 distinct host-polymer/salt systems. Applying the same pipeline to this new dataset, a tuned Random Forest reaches R2 = 0.47 under leave-one-out cross-validation, or 0.36 under a more conservative 5-fold estimate, well below the lithium benchmark.Through chemistry-informed feature engineering and a nested cross-validation check, we show this gap is driven primarily by data scarcity and literature measurement heterogeneity, not by model or feature choice. We argue the scarcity is itself the central finding: it puts a number, for the first time, on how far behind the multivalent and non-lithium polymer electrolyte literature sits relative to the lithium-ion mainstream. We release the curated dataset and pipeline to support future community data collection.

item.title: LatticeMind: A Validation-Gated Agentic Framework for Density Functional Theory Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.26869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-principles calculations are rarely single solver calls: they are multistage workflows in which structures, settings, and saved densities must pass correctly between dependent stages. Language models can write a valid single input, but reliability collapses once stages are chained: a dropped dependency, wrong file handoff, or hallucinated keyword can invalidate results even when the solver runs, and such errors surface only after costly execution. We introduce LatticeMind, a validation-gated agentic framework that converts natural-language requests into executable, checkable density functional theory (DFT) projects. A workflow contract specifies required stages, files, and dependencies; deterministic validators inspect the project before any solver launch; failed checks trigger bounded repair; and reports remain traceable to project files. On a 44-case RESCU benchmark spanning total-energy, density-of-states, band-structure, magnetic, phonon workflows, three non-flagship LLM backends reproduced every reference value; 119 of 132 runs passed on the first validated plan and the rest after one repair cycle. Ablations identify the workflow contract and pre-execution validation as the principal reliability mechanisms; a conventional trial-and-repair baseline reaches 71% at twice the token cost per success. The same architecture reproduces every reference value on a 19-case VASP benchmark, demonstrating transfer across solvers. Beyond these task families, LatticeMind generated and validated the 23 inputs of a multistage study of Rh-induced electronic responses at a Rh$_6$/In$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N photocatalyst interface. These results establish workflow contracts, deterministic validation, bounded repair, and traceable records as a practical foundation for reliable AI-assisted scientific computing, where preventable errors are caught before execution and the solver is never the first validator.

item.title: Heat-current-induced nonreciprocal phonon damping
item.description: arXiv:2610.27014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-reversal symmetry enforces equal equilibrium linewidths for time-reversed phonon modes at opposite wave vectors. Here we show that a steady heat current can produce nonreciprocal anharmonic damping even in centrosymmetric nonmagnetic crystals. The effect arises from nonequilibrium occupations of scattering partners, which change the statistical weights of time-reversed three-phonon channels while their squared matrix elements remain equal. Within the single-mode relaxation-time approximation, we derive a linewidth correction that is linear in the temperature gradient and odd under wave-vector reversal. The response depends on scattering-partner velocities and equilibrium lifetimes and retains signed channel weights absent from the equilibrium linewidth. First-principles calculations for centrosymmetric MgO and diamond yield nonzero, mode-dependent linewidth corrections at selected finite wave vectors, demonstrating the mechanism in both ionic and covalent crystals. Reversing the heat current at fixed local temperature exchanges the broadening and narrowing of paired modes. This current-reversible linewidth contrast provides a spectral signature of occupation feedback, with potential implications for nonlinear phonon transport.

item.title: MOFFieldBench: A Machine Learning Benchmark for Continuous Electronic Fields in Metal-Organic Frameworks
item.description: arXiv:2610.27036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning models for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) predominantly rely on atomic structures, whereas electron-density (ED) and electrostatic-potential (ESP) fields remain underexplored as scalable learning representations. These continuous fields encode complementary spatial and electronic information relevant to structure-property relationships, particularly pore geometry and guest-framework interactions, but costly first-principles calculations, storage requirements and the scarcity of systematically aligned datasets limit their broader use. Here we introduce MOFFieldBench, a multimodal benchmark comprising approximately 46,000 MOFs with one-to-one aligned crystallographic structures, ED fields and ESP fields. A unified workflow integrates field generation, error-controlled compression and sparse point-cloud representation, supporting field reconstruction, prediction of 13 material properties, multimodal property prediction and pairwise cross-modal retrieval. ED and ESP provide competitive representations for pore geometry, adsorption and separation properties. Multimodal fusion improves several prediction tasks relative to the best unimodal reference, supporting complementary predictive roles for atomic structures and electronic fields. Learned ED reconstruction closely approximates first-principles reference densities, while predicted-density initialization reduces self-consistent-field calculation time by 13.59\% on average in paired tests. These results support electronic fields as practical, informative learning modalities and establish MOFFieldBench as a resource for studying representation choice, multimodal learning and electronic-field-driven MOF modelling.

item.title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface
item.description: arXiv:2610.28254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.

item.title: Symmetry-Guided Machine Learning of Spin-Dependent Nonlinear Hall Response
item.description: arXiv:2610.28529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Berry-curvature dipole can produce a nonlinear Hall current even when the linear Hall response vanishes, but symmetry alone does not determine its magnitude or magnetic tunability. The interplay of structural symmetry, moment orientation, and carrier occupation is examined in a honeycomb model. Curvature maps and the band-summed dipole integrand reveal how velocity and the occupation window near the Fermi level select signed contributions. Removing threefold rotation permits a nonmagnetic dipole perpendicular to the surviving mirror. Generic magnetic reorientation activates the second component and tunes both components through positive and negative values. Global reversal preserves the dipole while reversing the intrinsic linear Hall conductivity, allowing a finite bulk dipole contribution from equally populated reversed domains under uniform-field averaging.A symmetry-constrained polynomial model predicts both dipole components for 256 held-out spin configurations, achieving coefficients of determination $R^2 > 0.9995$ at the reference chemical potential. At fixed carrier density, orientation-dependent shifts of the chemical potential modify the response and yield slightly larger prediction errors for the chosen model. Across the chemical-potential sweep,the prediction accuracy decreases more strongly for $D_y$,revealing an energy dependence of the surrogate's performance. Within semiclassical transport with a constant relaxation time, the calculated dipole determines the angular dependence of the quadratic current and its rectified and second-harmonic components. These results provide a quantitative representation of magnetic-orientation-dependent Berry-curvature dipoles and show how carrier occupation influences both the response and its predictability.

item.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.28629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

item.title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.27136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.

item.title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.27762v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

item.title: TexFlow: learning crystallographic texture on SO(3) manifold via normalizing flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.28363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Crystallographic texture is an important microstructural feature that statistically describes the orientations of grains in polycrystalline materials. Conventional texture analysis relies on the orientation distribution functions and pole figures, which are essential for interpreting the texture of a given material specimen but do not, by themselves, provide a direct framework for predictive modeling of process-structure-property linkages. Data- and machine learning-based approaches offer a means to address this gap; however, a key challenge lies in developing representations and learning frameworks that account for the manifold structure of rotations. In particular, many existing machine learning techniques are designed for Euclidean data and therefore are not readily applicable to rotations in the non-Euclidean group $\text{SO}(3)$. Here we introduce TexFlow, a conditional normalizing flow framework for texture modeling that learns a probability distribution over rotations in $\text{SO}(3)$ by construction. Rotations are encoded in a six-dimensional Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization representation which is then mapped back to valid rotations $\mathbf{R}\in\text{SO}(3)$. The framework supports conditional probabilistic modeling of texture $p(\mathbf{R}|c)$, where $c$ may represent processing parameters like temperature or deformation state. To complement conventional texture-analysis visualizations, such as pole figures and sections of the orientation distribution function, we further introduce Hopf-fibration visualizations as a compact global representation of texture. TexFlow is validated on both unconditional and conditional experimental and simulated texture datasets spanning diverse material systems. We show that TexFlow can accurately capture multimodal textures and their conditional evolution, providing a data-driven framework for establishing process-texture linkages.

item.title: Unveiling the Electronic Origin of Anomalous Contact Conductance in Twisted Bilayer Graphene
item.description: arXiv:2506.21721v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study theoretically investigates the contact conductance in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), addressing recent experimental observations from scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and conductive atomic force microscopy (c-AFM). These experiments revealed a surprising non-monotonic current pattern as a function of the TBG rotation angle $\theta$, with a peak at $\theta \approx 5^\circ$, a finding that markedly departs from the well-known magic angle TBG behavior. To elucidate this phenomenon, we develop a theoretical and computational framework {based on the system's local density of states, and evaluate the contact current over the energy range of states that contribute to the junction}. {Our results, obtained for both relaxed and rigid TBG structures, indicate that the conductance maximum at $\theta \approx 5^{\circ}$ is not primarily caused by structural relaxation or by changes in the AA-stacking area: the maximum persists, at essentially the same angle, in rigid (unreconstructed) lattices.} Instead, we attribute this peak to the evolution of the electronic band structure, specifically the shifting of van Hove singularities (vHs) toward the Fermi level as the twist angle decreases. The precise location of the maximum tracks the energy window of states participating in the contact, which in contact-mode measurements is set by the local doping under the metallic tip rather than by the small applied bias alone. We show that the angle of maximum conductance shifts with carrier doping, a dependence that is directly testable by electrostatic gating and that a purely structural mechanism cannot produce.

item.title: Strain-Dependent Wetting of Graphene
item.description: arXiv:2601.20134v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how water wets graphene is critical for predicting and controlling its behaviour in nanofluidic, sensing, and energy applications. A key measure of wetting is the contact angle made by a liquid droplet against the surface, yet experimental measurements for graphene span a wide range, with no consensus for free-standing graphene. Here, we use a machine learning potential with ab initio accuracy to provide an atomistic first-principles prediction for this unsolved problem, finding a weakly hydrophilic contact angle of $72.1 \pm 1.5 \deg$. More importantly, we unveil that graphene's wetting properties are highly sensitive to mechanical strain: tensile strain makes graphene significantly less hydrophilic, while compressive strain induces coherent ripples around the droplet, resulting in pronounced anisotropic wetting and contact angle hysteresis. We show that there is a strong coupling between the three-phase contact line and the intrinsic thermal ripples of free-standing graphene, which contributes to this strain sensitivity. Our results demonstrate that the wettability of 2D membranes are governed not only by their chemistry but also by their dynamic morphology, introducing a new class of wetting behaviour unique to atomically thin materials that offers an additional explanation for variability in experimental measurements. These findings reveal that mechanical strain may be a practical route to controlling wetting in 2D nanomaterials-based technologies, with promising consequences for nanofluidic and nano-filtration applications.

item.title: Electrohydraulic Fields Generated by Active Transport at Tissue Interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2605.22056v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Living cells and tissues can generate complex patterns of electric fields and fluid flows which can play important role in physiology. Both, fields and flows are rooted in ion transport across biological interfaces: cell membranes and epithelial cell layers. Here we develop a unified electrohydraulic framework that combines electric fields, osmotic pressures, and fluid flows, emphasising their couplings. We consider an active, permeable interface that drives electrohydraulic fields in the surrounding bulk. We show that spatially heterogeneous ion transport acts as a distributed current source, generating long-range electric fields, osmotic gradients, and fluid flows. Using this framework, we show that patterns of ion pumping at cell and tissue boundaries can simultaneously produce large-scale electric fields and fluid flows due to electrohydraulic coupling. A key insight is that an external electric field and an internal dipolar pumping pattern can be physically equivalent and can generate the same pattern of ion current and fluid flows. The induced dipolar osmotic pressure can drive self-propulsion through bulk osmotic coupling, with a mobility determined by interfacial permeability and system size, a mechanism distinct from classical electrophoresis or electro-osmosis. We further show that for strong fields a new effect emerges. Nonlinear coupling can lead to isotropic swelling of a hollow ball of cells. This can explain recent experiments on epithelial organoids. Finally, we show that feedback between ion transport and resulting electric fields can drive spontaneous symmetry breaking, generating dipolar or multipolar fields and patterns. Our work highlights the importance of electrohydraulic coupling in the emergence in currents and fields in the biological systems.

item.title: Tensor computing application programming interface: An application-oriented, lightweight API for portable high-performance tensor network computations
item.description: arXiv:2512.23917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tensor networks (TNs) are a central computational tool in quantum science and artificial intelligence. However, the lack of a unified software interface across tensor-computing frameworks severely limits the portability of TN applications, coupling algorithmic development to specific hardware and software back ends. To address this challenge, we introduce the Tensor Computing Application Programming Interface (TCAPI)---an application-oriented, lightweight API designed to enable framework-independent, high-performance TN applications, currently specified for \texttt{C++} and \texttt{Python}. TCAPI provides well-defined type-system conventions that abstract tensor objects, together with a minimal yet expressive set of core functions for essential tensor manipulations and tensor linear-algebra operations, with operation semantics shared across language specifications. Through numerical demonstrations of representative tensor-network applications implemented in \texttt{C++} using TCAPI, we show that code written against TCAPI can be migrated seamlessly across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms while achieving performance comparable to native framework implementations. We further provide open-source implementations of TCAPI based on \textit{Cytnx} and \textit{ITensor} in \texttt{C++}, and on \textit{NumPy} in \texttt{Python}, demonstrating its practicality and ease of integration with existing tensor-computing frameworks.

item.title: Wigner Time: from experimental intent to real-time laboratory control
item.description: arXiv:2609.06230v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Precisely timed, multi-device control in atomic, molecular and optical physics is provided by specialized real-time systems, which impose their own terms on the description of the experiment: a program over a global clock, in which every stage boundary is an absolute time computed from everything preceding it. Such descriptions are tightly coupled -- changing one stage affects all later ones -- and are correspondingly hard to reuse, inspect, or move elsewhere. We introduce Wigner Time, a Python package in which the experimental procedure is instead represented as data: a table of timed updates, assembled by composing functions and referred to named points in the experiment rather than to absolute instants. Hardware enters only at a final conversion step, leaving the description readable and back-end agnostic. Wigner Time has run two cold-atom setups for more than two years, where taking the computation out of the real-time program improved the achievable temporal resolution five-fold; the design applies to any domain requiring precise multi-device timing.

item.title: The surprising simplicity of forecasting quantum chaotic many-body dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.10697v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurately simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics remains a major computational challenge for classical methods, due to the rapid buildup and spatial spreading of entanglement during the evolution. This raises the question of whether machine learning can provide an effective alternative for predicting quantum dynamics. We address this question by formulating quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem, using a few-qubit PXP chain, realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays, as a benchmark. By varying the initial state, the system spans dynamical regimes ranging from ergodic behavior to quantum many-body scarring, providing a controlled setting for testing forecasting models across qualitatively different dynamics. We compare two contrasting architectures: an expressive nonlinear Transformer and DLinear, a simple linear forecasting model. The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the more ergodic regime, but its performance progressively deteriorates as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear remains accurate across the entire family of initial states, with its main deviations consisting of small high-frequency oscillations that have little effect on the overall prediction error. Remarkably, these results show that observables generated by complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast with high accuracy through a simple linear mapping from past to future observations. This reveals that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution need not translate into an equally complex forecasting problem.

item.title: Symmetry-Guided Machine Learning of Spin-Dependent Nonlinear Hall Response
item.description: arXiv:2610.28529v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Berry-curvature dipole can produce a nonlinear Hall current even when the linear Hall response vanishes, but symmetry alone does not determine its magnitude or magnetic tunability. The interplay of structural symmetry, moment orientation, and carrier occupation is examined in a honeycomb model. Curvature maps and the band-summed dipole integrand reveal how velocity and the occupation window near the Fermi level select signed contributions. Removing threefold rotation permits a nonmagnetic dipole perpendicular to the surviving mirror. Generic magnetic reorientation activates the second component and tunes both components through positive and negative values. Global reversal preserves the dipole while reversing the intrinsic linear Hall conductivity, allowing a finite bulk dipole contribution from equally populated reversed domains under uniform-field averaging.A symmetry-constrained polynomial model predicts both dipole components for 256 held-out spin configurations, achieving coefficients of determination $R^2 > 0.9995$ at the reference chemical potential. At fixed carrier density, orientation-dependent shifts of the chemical potential modify the response and yield slightly larger prediction errors for the chosen model. Across the chemical-potential sweep,the prediction accuracy decreases more strongly for $D_y$,revealing an energy dependence of the surrogate's performance. Within semiclassical transport with a constant relaxation time, the calculated dipole determines the angular dependence of the quadratic current and its rectified and second-harmonic components. These results provide a quantitative representation of magnetic-orientation-dependent Berry-curvature dipoles and show how carrier occupation influences both the response and its predictability.

item.description: In a recent issue of Nature Nanotechnology, Liu, Zhang, Wang, and co-workers report an in situ yttrium doping strategy that forms lanthanum-yttrium-oxide (LYO) interphases at garnet solid electrolyte grain boundaries. The lithiophobic LYO interphases improve fracture toughness and mitigate electronic leakage, collectively enhancing dendrite resistance and supporting cathode integration.

item.title: Complementary Roles of Iodide-Mediated Pathways and Anion Dynamics in Lithium-Ion Transport in Li3PS4-LiI Glasses
item.description: LiI addition enhances lithium-ion transport in sulfide glasses, yet the microscopic mechanisms linking halide incorporation to faster conduction remain unclear. Here, we investigate how LiI promotes Li+ migration in (100−x)Li3PS4–xLiI glasses by resolving changes in local structure, migration energetics, and anion dynamics. A machinelearning potential trained on newly generated ab initio molecular dynamics data and an existing sulfide-electrolyte dataset enables 10 ns simulations of approximately 5000atom glass models at 300 K over a LiI content range of 0–50 mol%. The potential is validated against density functional theory calculations, experimental densities, and X-ray total scattering profiles. Although the PS4 3–units remain intact and their time-averaged inter-unit correlations change little, Li+ diffusivity more than doubles across this composition range, accompanied by increased migration beyond local cage-like regions. To characterize the energetics of these pathways in a disordered environment, we introduce an analysis that combines Voronoi partitioning into P-and I–-centered domains with atomic potentialenergy fluctuations along Li+ trajectories. The resulting statistical local energy-barrier indicators allow comparisons between domain transitions without assigning absolute activation energies. This analysis reveals two complementary effects of LiI addition. Transitions involving I–-centered domains exhibit lower barrier indicators than direct transitions between P-centered domains, identifying favorable I–-mediated migration pathways. LiI addition also lowers the barrier indicators for direct P-to-P transitions, extending its influence beyond pathways that pass through I–-centered domains. Enhanced local translational and rotational dynamics of PS4 3–units accompany this broader reduction, suggesting that anion motion helps facilitate Li+ migration. These findings explain how LiI can enhance transport while largely preserving the average glass structure and highlight the combined roles of local migration pathways and anion dynamics in designing sulfide glass electrolytes.

item.title: Cristobalite-Type Compounds for Rechargeable Potassium-Ion Batteries
item.description: Potassium-ion batteries have emerged as high-voltage and economically advantageous electrochemical energy storage systems with promise to viably complement and/or augment lithium-ion technology owing to the natural abundance, projected low cost and favourable redox potential of potassium. Their continued advancement, however, is primarily predicated upon the discovery of electrode and electrolyte materials adept to delivering high energy density, long-term cycling stability and rigorous safety performance. Cristobalite-type compounds have recently garnered traction as prospective candidates, for these materials not only combine theoretically high energy density with structural robustness but can also be designed exclusively from earth-abundant and low-toxicity constituent elements. This Review provides a critical assessment of the rapidly expanding family of cristobalite-type compounds, which exhibit pronounced structural versatility and the capacity to reversibly intercalate two potassium ions per formula unit, thereby enabling high theoretical energy densities. We particularly survey recent advances in their structural chemistry, electrochemical behaviour and potassium-ion transport properties, and elucidate the mechanistic principles that govern their electrochemical performance. Finally, we outline future research directions, encompassing rational materials design, advanced characterisation methodologies and large-scale computational screening, to optimise cristobalite-type compounds as high-performance electrode materials and solid-state electrolytes for potassium-ion batteries.

item.title: Metasurface information processor based on 4D bionic hardware and software for ultralow energy consumption computing
item.description: As AI technology faces an energy crisis, one promising solution is bionic ultra-low energy computing hardware, which can operate at a power level as low as sub-20-watt based on the 4D model of Ca 2+ channels recently verified in brain information processing. Inspired by this model, here we design and fabricate a 4D bionic computing system based on information metasurface array with the powerful capability of electromagnetic controls. Paired with specific algorithms, each metasurface cell functions as a multifunctional unit, capable of storing, regulating, transmitting, and computing information simultaneously. The metasurface array also has high energy efficiency and precision required for high-performance bionic computing. Integrated with the DNA computing, this system is expected to achieve a variety of functions including DNA replication, DNA logical computation, and DNA produce/readout. We aim to pave the way for a new paradigm in advanced computational materials that meet the evolving demands of AI and robotics.

item.title: A grouped split silently removes the chemistry entangled with its grouping variable: the case of MOF topology hold-out
item.description: Machine learning screens metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO2 capture, and 2026 studies on enumerated databases have converged on topology hold-out as a test of topological transferability, presupposing untested separability of topology and chemistry. They are not: on hMOF (324,426 structures), 74.7% of coarse compositions (61.3% of structures) occur in a single topology, and for seven of hMOF's eleven topologies removing one topology leaves every structure with no chemical counterpart in training; the confound replicates on ARC-MOF (99.3% coarse single-topology), which is not independent of hMOF, so only a leave-one-source-out bound (98.6–99.8%) is claimed. On the isoreticular pcu ↔ nbo pair, removing the matched topology degrades nbo-side MAE by 70.0% while a sizematched control leaves it unchanged, and across the shared 25,000-sample support set the top-1% hit rate falls from 50.4% to 19.3% (five seeds). Yet the topology penalty is not explained by chemistry alone: holding out the composite chemistry key instead retains R2 = 0.674 against topology's 0.379, so the composition counts fix the identity of the withheld chemistry, not its cost. Topology hold-out should therefore not be read as a clean test of topological transferability, and grouped-split reports should first disclose the confound structure and chemical granularity, for which we provide a reporting checklist.

item.title: Grassmannian Density Learning for Physically Consistent Kohn–Sham Electronic Structure Prediction
item.description: Deep-learning electronic-structure models show great potential to accelerate first-principles calculations, with broad implications for materials science, biology and drug discovery. Yet no consensus has emerged on which physical quantity should be modeled to represent electronic states. As two fundamental quantities that arise naturally in Kohn–Sham density functional theory, the Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian and electronic density have attracted the most attention. Hamiltonian prediction, however, devotes substantial modeling capacity to degrees of freedom that do not affect the occupied electronic subspace, whereas direct regression of density matrices or real-space densities removes this redundancy but cannot ensure that the prediction represents a physically admissible electronic state. Motivated by the fact that electronic states themselves reside on a constrained manifold, we observe that predicting coordinates directly on this manifold can simultaneously eliminate redundant degrees of freedom and preserve physical admissibility. Here we introduce GeoK, a framework that predicts compact occupied–virtual orbital-rotation generators as coordinates on the manifold of electronic states, thereby ensuring each prediction corresponds to a valid electronic state of the target molecular system. We further develop a neural-network architecture tailored to this geometric prediction task. Across in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks, as well as downstream applications, GeoK consistently improves electronic-state prediction over the evaluated Hamiltonian and unconstrained densityregression baselines, while supporting robust deployment in downstream first-principles workflows. These results establish orbital-rotation generator prediction as a principled and reliable paradigm for intrinsic electronic-state modeling, opening a route towards more accurate and transferable deep-learning electronic-structure models.

item.title: ProtBed: a streamlined web platform for exploratory statistics and predictive modeling in quantitative mass spectrometry
item.description: Mass spectrometry proteomics and metabolomics generate high-dimensional quantitative matrices requiring rigorous statistical and machine learning evaluation, yet existing analytical workflows typically depend on programmatic scripting or remote cloud servers that introduce datagovernance constraints. ProtBed is a client-side web application that executes post-extraction data exploration directly in the browser runtime. The platform integrates deterministic preprocessing, pairwise and omnibus hypothesis testing, six-model cross-validated machine learning, and publication-ready visualization while preserving complete local custody of quantitative abundance matrices and clinical metadata. Empirical validation was conducted across four diverse cohorts totaling 250 clinical specimens. On an untargeted GC-MS urine cohort (𝑛 = 40; 356 metabolites), stratified five-fold cross-validated classifiers discriminated diabetic kidney disease with AUC = 0.90 (89% sensitivity, 82% specificity). In a deep-coverage post-mortem substantia nigra tissue cohort (𝑛 = 30; 9,606 quantified proteins), full-matrix modeling achieved out-of-fold AUC = 0.99 using logistic regression (AUC = 0.96 for linear support vector machines) and prioritized neuroinflammatory mediators including SAA1, CRP, and GFAP. ProtBed further resolved multiclass diagnostic arms in plasma extracellular-vesicle proteomics (𝑛 = 124) and characterized dysregulated lipid classes in Alzheimer's disease plasma (𝑛 = 56). ProtBed is freely accessible at https://protbed.com/.

item.title: Combinatorial Steiner Methodology for Efficiently Exploring Chemical Space in CO2 Hydrogenation to Fischer-Tropsch Reactivity via High-throughput Experimentation
item.description: High-throughput experimentation (HTE) and machine learning (ML) have accelerated discovery in molecular chemistry. Meanwhile, such advances in heterogeneous catalysis are hindered by the complexity of materials and the vast chemical space. We present a mathematically optimized methodology using Steiner coverings to explore multi-component catalysts and access lower-dimension interactions through higher-dimension blocks. From 21 elements, we designed a library of 70 trimetallic mixed-metal-oxide catalysts, covering all 210 possible bimetallic pairs. The experimental workflow was automated by a robotic platform and applied to thermocatalytic CO2 hydrogenation, critical for achieving a circular carbon economy. In just 70 materials we successfully recovered and uncovered trends in methanation, reverse water–gas shift (RWGS), and methanol synthesis, while discovering a highly active FeGaRu catalyst for CO2–Fischer–Tropsch synthesis that retains this reactivity when simplified to binary FeRu, Ga providing improved performances. Our combinatorial optimization methodology replaces thousands of manual experiments with strategic exploration, improving the discovery rate for complex, multi-component heterogeneous catalysts.
