item.title: Advancing Targeted Nanoparticle mRNA Delivery Using Machine Learning
item.description: Effective delivery remains a major barrier to translating nucleic acid therapeutics into the clinic. A successful delivery system must cross biological barriers, target the tissue of interest, deliver the potent payload to the cell, and be manufactured with ease at scale. The three clinically relevant carrier classes involve trade-offs with one another: viral vectors are limited by payload capacity and limited redosing; lipid nanoparticles are a clinical standard for mRNA delivery, but default to liver tropism; polymeric nanoparticles have lower immunogenicity and offer shelf-stable manufacturing, but fewer candidates have reached clinical trials. The design of effective nanomedicines requires multi-faceted optimization of nanoparticle properties, targeted delivery, and cargo efficacy. Machine learning offers an opportunity to accelerate nanoparticle development by effectively navigating the design space and providing a deeper insight into structure-activity relationships. Here, we present a high-level overview of the fast evolving nanoparticle delivery field and outline best practices for advancing the development of targeted nanoparticle mRNA delivery using machine learning. The key design principles are introduced: identification of target cell surface receptors, de novo design of epitope-targeted antibodies, design of mRNA payloads, and prediction of nanoparticle properties and their interactions at different biological scales. Together, advancing targeted nanoparticle mRNA delivery will require a coordinated integration of key design principles, the generation of high-quality datasets, and the effective adoption of machine learning.

item.title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.18967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $\nu = 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

item.title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.19404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

item.title: A practical route to amorphous solid-state electrolyte structures by hybrid reverse Monte Carlo with foundation potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.19846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Amorphous alkali oxychlorides are fast ion conductors, but their atomic structure remains unresolved. Total scattering sums all partial pair correlations into one curve that has no unique inversion, so the structure must be modeled. Melt-quench molecular dynamics builds a model from the interatomic potential alone, and reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) builds one from the measurement alone. The two have rarely been compared with all else held fixed. We benchmark both routes and two hybrid schemes on amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}} against one neutron pair distribution function with one foundation potential. The hybrid schemes put the energy either in the acceptance rule (inline) or in short relaxations between blocks of refinement (alternating). Each refinement starts from a melt-quench glass or from a random packing of isolated units. The glass has the lowest energy and places the first-shell peaks correctly, but carries almost none of the oscillation beyond 6~\AA{} (goodness of fit $R^{2} = 0.29$). Pure RMC fits the measurement to within its counting noise ($R^{2} = 0.99$), but at more than $1.3$~eV/atom above the glass, and niobium loses about half of its first-shell chlorine. Started from the glass, both hybrid schemes reach $R^{2} = 0.92$ within $0.1$~eV/atom of its energy and keep its coordination chemistry. Structures from the two inputs fit almost equally well and differ in energy by a tenth of the RMC penalty, yet they differ in whether their polyhedra are connected. The input is therefore part of the method. We recommend quenching a glass with a foundation potential and refining it against the measurement with a hybrid scheme. The resulting structure carries both the local chemistry and the medium-range order, and it is the starting point for modeling ion transport in these conductors.

item.title: Deep Learning of Phase Transitions for Bilinear-Biquadratic Spin-1 Chains from Correlation Aspects
item.description: arXiv:2610.19995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the role of different correlation functions in reconstructing the phase diagram of the spin-1 bilinear-biquadratic chain, parametrized by the angle $\theta$ between the bilinear and biquadratic couplings, using our previously developed label-free machine-learning pipeline \cite{Ming21, Ming23}, in which an autoencoder compresses iDMRG correlation matrices into latent features and K-means clustering with silhouette analysis groups them into phases. Without any prior labels, the scheme reveals four natural phases, the Haldane, dimerized, critical trimerized, and ferromagnetic phases, and accurately locates the Takhtajan-Babujian ($\theta=-\pi/4$), $SU(3)$-symmetric Uimin-Lai-Sutherland ($\theta=\pi/4$), and Ferro-Dimer ($\theta=5\pi/4$) transition points; a shallow supervised refinement further sharpens the phase boundaries. We find that different correlation functions play fundamentally different roles in phase identification. The $SU(3)$-symmetric correlation alone selects a four-cluster partition that can be associated with the four phases, whereas the spin-spin and dimer-dimer correlations must be combined to recover the complete phase diagram. In contrast, the trimer-trimer correlation behaves as a marginal correlation: it is insufficient for phase identification by itself but improves the precision of the predicted phase boundaries when combined with the other correlations. Furthermore, the latent representations and silhouette values reveal signatures that we relate to the $\theta$ dependence of the correlations within each phase and, tentatively, to the underlying renormalization-group structure. These results demonstrate that machine learning can not only identify quantum phases but also uncover the physical information encoded in different correlation functions.

item.title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.20063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.

item.title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.20374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in polymer synthesis and computational modeling are expanding the block-copolymer architecture space accessible for phase-behavior design. Machine learning can accelerate this exploration, yet a common representation capable of learning across diverse chain topologies remains lacking. Here, we present a graph neural network (GNN) representation of acyclic AB multiblock architectures, tested by random-phase approximation (RPA) instability prediction. Each chain is represented as a graph, enabling a common model to learn across diverse topologies. This representation, which organizes RPA-related information, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks and demonstrates its potential for reuse across tasks through transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction. By effectively linking block-copolymer chain architecture to field-theoretic response, this graph representation not only reconstructs stability-limit curves but also provides a practical route for future self-consistent field theory exploration of ordered phase space across complex topologies.

item.title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.19919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

item.title: Magnon Kerr Effect in a Magnetic Thin Film Strongly Coupled to a Microwave Resonator
item.description: arXiv:2601.22271v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Progress in cavity magnonics relies on tunable nonlinearities in magnon-photon interactions for controlling magnon dynamics and frequency conversion. Here, we demonstrate the magnon Kerr effect in anisotropic magnonic systems comprising iron garnet thin films coupled to a loop-gap microwave resonator. The strong shape anisotropy, combined with strain, enhances the magnon Kerr effect compared to a sphere of equivalent volume by up to three orders of magnitude, while the cavity enables sensitive probing of magnetization dynamics. We demonstrate continuous tunability of the magnitude and sign of the Kerr shift by controlling the static orientation of the magnetization, in excellent agreement with theory. Our findings demonstrate a scalable approach to enhancing Kerr anharmonicity in hybrid magnon-photon systems while preserving coherent magnon-photon interactions.

item.title: Gap-controlled thermalization in a SSH model version of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chain
item.description: arXiv:2609.09498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In classical anharmonic lattices, the resonance structure driving nonlinear mode mixing is reshaped by band gaps. However, it remains unclear whether a spectral gap hinders or promotes long-time thermalization. Here we study a dimerized Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chain - a classical SSH model analogue with alternating spring constants - and quantify how the acoustic-optical gap controls relaxation under alpha-type (cubic) nonlinearity. Tracking modal energies and spectral entropy via long-time symplectic simulations, we find a sharp isolation threshold when the dimerization strength reaches half its maximum value, set by the onset of the first umklapp process that allows two zone-boundary acoustic phonons to fuse into a zone-center optical phonon; below this threshold, three-wave acoustic-acoustic-optical scattering activates the optical branch on timescales of order 1e4 oscillation periods, while above it the bands remain dynamically isolated. We further show that boundary conditions reshape this picture, producing long-lived sticky states for specific mode excitations. These results establish the phononic gap as a tunable, momentum-selective filter for nonlinear energy transport, suggesting a general route to controlling thermalization in dimerized or topologically gapped nonlinear lattices.

item.title: Depth-aware machine learning for 3D reconstruction of fibrous porous electrodes by FIB-SEM tomography
item.description: Quantitative three-dimensional reconstruction of porous polymers with sub-micrometer feature sizes is central to understanding and designing electrochemical interfaces and membranes. However, focused ion beam–scanning electron microscopy tomography combined with conventional segmentation techniques cannot readily recon-struct complex disordered morphologies such as fibers. Standard segmentation workflows misclassify out-ofplane material as in-plane material, distorting the reconstructed pore network, fiber connectivity, and interfacial area. Here, we introduce an annotation-free, depth-aware machine-learning framework that combines monocular depth estimation, trained on real-scale images, with unsupervised clustering to separate exposed polymer crosssections from subsurface contributions in serial FIB–SEM tomography images. Applied to copper-coated electro-spun poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) fiber mats, the approach produces 3D reconstructions that preserve fibrous morphology more faithfully than conventional supervised and unsupervised segmentation. Quan-titative validation against capillary flow porometry, pycnometry, and high-resolution wide-angle X-ray computed tomography demonstrates improved agreement across pore diameter, fiber volume ratio, and copper-depth distribution metrics. This work establishes depth-aware segmentation as a transferable strategy from real-scale to nanoscale imaging, requiring no labelled training data and enabling accurate 3D segmentation and reconstruction from SEM images. This approach opens a path toward more reliable structure–property relationships in disordered porous polymer materials.

item.title: PolyNet: A Python Package for Polymer Informatics
item.description: Polymers are used in a wide range of industries for diverse applications but formulating them to attain desired properties remains a challenging task. Polymer informatics has emerged as a powerful approach for the rational design of materials. Here, we present PolyNet, an open-source Python package that provides an end-to-end workflow for polymer informatics. PolyNet: 1) reads and validates datasets of polymer properties, including the monomer structures and their molar ratios; 2) creates vector- and graph-based representations of the polymers; 3) trains and optimises traditional machine learning (ML) models and graph neural networks (GNNs); 4) compares representations and models statistically; 5) deploys the models to screen in silico libraries of polymers, flagging polymers outside the applicability domain of the models and estimating their expected prediction error; and 6) interprets the models to understand structure–property relationships. PolyNet provides unique features such as: modelling of homopolymers and copolymers with any number of components, using the molar ratio of monomers in both vector- and graph-based representations; acceptance of textual representations of monomers or repeating units; calculation of polyBERT fingerprints and PolyMetriX and RDKit descriptors and fingerprints and accepting standalone user precalculated representations; benchmarking of all representation–model combinations on identical data splits using paired statistical tests; and chemically interpretable explanations through fragment-level attribution for GNNs and SHAP analysis for traditional ML models. Every experiment automatically records its configuration, data splits, hyperparameter search spaces and trained models, supporting full reproducibility in line with FAIR principles. PolyNet can be used through Python scripts, a command-line interface, or a graphical user interface for researchers without programming experience. We exemplify PolyNet by two case studies: glass transition temperature prediction for homopolymers, where cluster-based data splits showed that random splits overestimate model performance, the applicability domain identified less reliable predictions, and the model explanations recovered the known effect of chain mobility on Tg; and ¹⁹F MRI signal-to-noise ratio prediction for copolymers, where encoding monomer molar ratios is key to accurate predictions.

item.title: Halide Exchange via Perovskite Nanocrystals for Interfacial Defect Passivation in Solar Cells
item.description: Metal halide perovskites have emerged as leading candidates for next-generation optoelectronics, with perovskite solar cells (PSCs) achieving power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) exceeding 26%. However, solution-processed hybrid perovskite films typically suffer from non-radiative recombination and ion migration driven by surface and interfacial defects, limiting device performance, fill factor, and long-term stability. To address these bottlenecks, we report a novel, scalable interface engineering strategy utilizing bromide-rich perovskite nanocrystals to modify 3D perovskite film surfaces via self-driven solid-state halide exchange. The resulting surface-graded heterojunction passivates key iodide vacancies, suppresses ion migration, and optimizes charge extraction. Consequently, modified PSCs demonstrate a ~5% boost in short-circuit current density () and an improved fill factor of 75.3%, driving a ~10% relative increase in PCE from 20.13% (control) to 22.19%. This simple, single-step nanocrystal treatment provides a promising pathway toward robust, scalable, and high-efficiency optoelectronic architectures.

item.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Subsequent Drug Release Trajectories using Early Release Information in PLGA Microparticles
item.description: Accurate prediction of drug-release behavior from PLGA microparticles may reduce the experimental effort required for formulation characterization, yet conventional prediction approaches rely primarily on static molecular and formulation descriptors and do not incorporate experimentally observed release behavior as it becomes available during an ongoing experiment. Here, we develop a machine-learning framework that integrates molecular and formulation descriptors with early-release measurements to predict subsequent drug-release trajectories from PLGA microparticles. A dataset comprising 4,913 release observations from 321 formulations was analyzed using random forest regression with formulation-grouped cross-validation. Using a common set of 89 formulations, we systematically evaluated the predictive value of increasing amounts of early-release information. Prediction accuracy improved with additional early measurements, but the incremental benefit progressively diminished, with two and three measurements capturing 64.7% and 91.9% of the total predictive gain achieved with four measurements, respectively. The value of early information also varied substantially across formulations, with greater benefits generally observed for formulations that were more difficult to predict from static descriptors alone. Trajectory-level analysis further revealed that early observations constrained subsequent release trajectories to different extents across formulations. These findings demonstrate that experimentally observed early-release behavior provides formulation-specific predictive information beyond static descriptors and establish a data-driven framework for quantifying information sufficiency in drug-release characterization.

item.title: Validation Design Governs the Apparent Predictive Performance of Machine Learning for PLGA Drug Release
item.description: Reliable generalization is essential for machine-learning models intended to predict drug-release behavior across heterogeneous experimental settings. However, multi-study experimental data often contain closely related formulations generated under shared materials, processing conditions, release protocols, and laboratory practices, creating hidden dependencies between training and test data. Such dependencies can make model performance appear stronger than its ability to generalize to genuinely new experimental domains. Here, we examine how validation topology governs the apparent predictability of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) microparticle drug release using a public dataset containing 321 formulations and 4,913 release observations collected across 113 studies. Using a common LightGBM prediction framework, we compare validation schemes ranging from random observation splitting to strict study-grouped holdout. Predictive performance decreases markedly as train–test independence becomes more stringent, with 𝑅! declining from 0.939 under random point splitting to 0.616–0.625 under formulation-level holdout and 0.372 when entire studies are withheld. Controlled overlap experiments further show that retaining samestudy sibling formulations in the training set systematically increases apparent performance, while nearest-neighbor analysis reveals lower prediction error for formulations lying closer to the training distribution, particularly when their nearest training counterpart originates from the same study. These results show that formulation-level independence alone does not ensure experimental-domain independence and demonstrate that apparent drug-release predictability is strongly conditioned by validation design. Study-aware validation therefore provides a more rigorous basis for assessing generalization of machine-learning models trained on heterogeneous multi-study experimental data.

item.title: Metasurface information processor based on 4D bionic hardware and software for ultralow energy consumption computing
item.description: As AI technology faces an energy crisis, one promising solution is bionic ultra-low energy computing hardware, which can operate at a power level as low as sub-20-watt based on the 4D model of Ca 2+ channels recently verified in brain information processing. Inspired by this model, here we design and fabricate a 4D bionic computing system based on information metasurface array with the powerful capability of electromagnetic controls. Paired with specific algorithms, each metasurface cell functions as a multifunctional unit, capable of storing, regulating, transmitting, and computing information simultaneously. The metasurface array also has high energy efficiency and precision required for high-performance bionic computing. Integrated with the DNA computing, this system is expected to achieve a variety of functions including DNA replication, DNA logical computation, and DNA produce/readout. We aim to pave the way for a new paradigm in advanced computational materials that meet the evolving demands of AI and robotics.
